│ Tier 1: the memo already exists. WorkspaceUsageGraphCache (analyzer/usages/workspace_graph_cache.rs) caches exactly the
│ file-major resolution pass, keyed by whole-workspace content identity. The usage_graph and most_relevant_files tools share it;
│ the policy evaluator just never consumes it. Wiring batch evaluation to that cache means the world is resolved once per content
│ state, and every query against unchanged content reuses it. Its limits are the interesting part: in-process only, 32 MiB
│ retention, and the invalidation is all-or-nothing — touch one file and the key (whole-workspace identity) misses, so you rebuild
│ everything.
│
│ Tier 2: your file-level memo, done soundly. The naive version — cache "file F's resolved outbound edges" by F's content hash —
│ is unsound, because resolution isn't a function of the file alone: add or remove a declaration elsewhere and F's references can
│ re-bind (that's precisely why reference_edges.rs refuses to persist a resolved third graph). The fix is to split the work by its
│ actual dependencies:
│
│ • Occurrence extraction (identifier, span, enclosing declaration, syntactic role) is blob-local, so it caches forever under the
│   store's existing content-addressed scheme. That's the expensive parse-and-walk half, paid once per blob ever.
│
│ • Binding depends on the definition landscape — but only on a characterizable slice of it: the resolution answers for the
│   identifiers this file mentions, given its imports. So persist the resolved edges alongside a resolution-environment digest: a
│   hash of the definition-lookup answers for exactly this blob's mentioned identifiers and import targets. On a commit, a file's
│   edges are reusable iff its digest still matches; the files whose digests could have changed are found through the existing
│   reverse identifier index — the same index the usage machinery already uses in the other direction. Wildcard imports widen a
│   file's environment (the digest must cover package-content answers), and dynamically-scoped languages widen it more; the edge
│   rows' existing proof/completeness labels let the cache be honest about that rather than silently wrong.
│
│ The resulting cost profile is the materialized-view-with-incremental-maintenance shape: first query (or an index-time warm task)
│ resolves the world once; afterwards, repo-wide aggregations like the extension-axis count are indexed SQL reads, and a typical
│ commit re-resolves only its changed blobs plus their mention-neighborhood. Resolver behavior changes invalidate through the same
│ epoch/generation salting every other derived fact already uses.

│ • The usual benefit of a crates.io dependency — receiving upstream fixes — is gone: the project is archived and you're
│   exact-pinning anyway. What remains is only "didn't copy the code," while the costs (schema shaped by upstream arena internals,
│   interop with types you keep private to bifrost-analysis, fork-on-first-bug) stay.
│ • You're already committed to building a from-scratch engine as the composition oracle. Promoting that to production, with lazy
│   SQL hydration bolted on, leaves upstream with no load-bearing role.
│ • Bifrost-specific needs — revision-selected hydration, deterministic cancellation quanta, ResolutionWitness recording — would
│   all be wrappers around upstream's stitcher regardless, so you'd own the hard integration surface either way.
│ 2. The performance bet is falsified last; move it early. Whole-workspace streaming with no persisted edges and no cache is
│ precisely the point the issue predicts will fail, yet the first realistic broad-consumer benchmark lands after three engines,
│ the Java spike, SQL persistence, and consumer routing. Note also the comparison baseline: today usage_graph/relevance hit a warm
│ whole-workspace cache (WorkspaceUsageRankingGraph + workspace_graph_cache.rs, 32 MiB retained), so warm repeated queries are

│ usage_graph/missing_tests-shaped full-workspace pass against both the cold pathological case and today's warm cached path, and

│ 3. Semantic refinement is the hardest component and gets one sentence. Stack graphs alone cannot resolve x.foo() without
│ receiver typing; the current per-language resolvers (11 *_graph strategy modules plus the per-language get_definition modules)
│ embed that logic today. "Persisted-fact semantic refinement for receivers, overloads, hierarchy, visibility, traits, macros" is
│ where the old resolvers' hardest parts either get reused or re-implemented — and your first cutover domain, Rust with
│ function-level missing_tests, is the worst case (traits, method calls, macros). The ExecPlan needs, per domain: which refinement
│ facts exist today, which are new, and whether refinement filters stitched candidates or the graph itself encodes type-scoped
